records.name: Gabon
records.summary: Gabon demands real caution — and on a surprising positive trajectory: after briefly criminalising same-sex intimacy in 2019, it decriminalised in 2020, and in November 2024 voters ratified a new constitution that rejected calls to criminalise homosexuality. No LGR; social conservatism; but the constitutional debate is now public and the pro-criminalisation side lost.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): criminalised same-sex intimacy in 2019 (max 6 months + US$8,561 fine), repealed in 2020 after Senate approval — reversal sharply divided public opinion; Nov-2024 constitution (military regime since Aug-2023) codifies privacy (Art.18) but retains Art.16 marriage definition; no legal gender recognition, LGBTI groups cannot register; same-sex relations legal for men and women per its country page (with caveat that criminalisation remains 'No' nationwide only since the 2020 repeal).

Erasing 76 Crimes (25 Nov 2024): Gabon's new constitution was ratified by referendum 16 Nov 2024 (over 90% yes, ~55% turnout) and rejected civil-society demands to re-criminalise homosexuality, adding LGBT+-protective privacy provisions — but codifies a marriage definition excluding same-sex couples. Context: Aug-2023 military coup ended 56 years of Bongo-family rule.

US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for Gabon: official assessment covering the year the new penal code criminalised same-sex conduct - documents the legal change and societal discrimination.

LGBTQ Nation (13 Dec 2019): Gabon criminalised same-sex relations by law passed quietly in July 2019 — up to 6 months + 5m CFA francs (~US$8,500); two men already arrested and released only after paying police bribes; Gabon inherited no colonial-era sodomy law (independence 1960). Enforcement precedent: arrests occurred within months of enactment — later reversed by the 2020 repeal.
Washington Blade (July 2020): Gabon formally decriminalised homosexuality - the National Assembly overturned the 2019 ban, restoring the pre-2019 status where same-sex conduct was not criminal.

Gabon Review (29 Oct 2019, French): Law 042/2018 of 5 Jul 2019 (new penal code) criminalises same-sex relations without naming 'homosexuality' — Art.402 files 'les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe' under 'atteintes aux mœurs' (sexual assaults/attacks on morals); earlier Dec-2013 police arrest of two alleged 'gay marriers' released. Primary-source detail on the criminalisation year (2019) later reversed in 2020.

records.name: Republic of the Congo
records.summary:
The Republic of the Congo is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised) — but the 2024 official assessment (EUAA COI) documented societal discrimination, police harassment (including bribes extracted under an ambiguous 'acts against nature' provision) and the absence of protection; there is no legal gender recognition, and only a small underground community.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure to a criminalisation regime, but the ambiguous under-21 'shameless act / acts against nature' provision has been used to justify discrimination and, in police practice, to extract bribes; no arrests or prosecutions under it were reported in 2022 or 2023.

sources.summary: EUAA COI Query Response Q29 (May 2024) on the Republic of the Congo: systematic review of legislation, implementation, treatment by state and society, and availability of state protection for LGBTQI+ people. Key findings: no law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between adults; Penal Code Article 331 (per ILGA) sets age of consent at 21 for same-sex vs 18 for different-sex acts; the under-21 'shameless act / against nature' provision's scope as applied to same-sex conduct is 'ambiguous', and sources say it is used to justify discrimination.

US State Department 2022 human rights report (Republic of the Congo), SOGI section: no law specifically prohibits consensual same-sex conduct between adults; a provision punishes 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under age 21 (6 months–3 years plus fine), scope ambiguous and not invoked for prosecutions. Police at times cite the provision to extract bribes from gay men; local NGOs reported violence, psychological/physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by government and nonstate actors.

US State Department 2023 human rights report (Republic of the Congo): no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the ambiguous under-21 provision during 2023; police continued using the 'act against nature' law as a pretext to solicit bribes from men; NGOs reported continuing psychological/physical harassment and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by both government actors and nonstate actors, with no anti-discrimination protections in law.

records.name: Burundi
records.summary: Burundi is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Same-sex conduct has been criminalised since 2009 (2 years), and the head of state himself has called for mob violence: in December 2023, President Ndayishimiye said LGBT people should be “taken to a stadium and stoned” because “that's what they deserve” — condemned by HRW as stoking fear; the Iteka League called it a call to lynching. There is no LGR, no community infrastructure (the oldest rights group works from exile), and arbitrary detention is routine.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (Jan 2024): 'Burundi President Stokes Fear Among LGBT People' — President Ndayishimiye's call to 'stone' homosexuals; HRW urges the ruling party to renounce persecution.

SOS Médias Burundi (Jan 2024): after President Évariste Ndayishimiye called for 'homosexuals to be stoned', LGBTQ Burundians reported terror; the Iteka League (in exile) called the remarks 'a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people'. Members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described the remarks as 'a real license to kill (us)'. Same-sex relations are criminalised in Burundi.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Burundi: documents the country's crisis (extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention, media shutdowns) and includes the section on acts of violence and discrimination against LGBT persons - same-sex conduct criminalised since 2009, with arrests and harassment documented.
US State Department 2009 Human Rights Report for Burundi (archived): covers the year the penal code criminalised same-sex conduct; documents discrimination against gays and lesbians.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Burundi: lists discrimination against gays and lesbians among common human-rights abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture and harsh prison conditions.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Burundi: documents torture, extrajudicial executions, prolonged pretrial detention, and discrimination against LGBT persons under the criminalised framework.

records.name: Central African Republic
records.summary:
The Central African Republic is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, and public same-sex affection display is criminalised under public-morals provisions — the current overview per freshness — while national administration barely exists outside the capital: armed groups control most areas, mob violence and police extortion against perceived LGBT people are documented, legal gender recognition is not permitted, and there is no community infrastructure.

For a visitor: nothing protects, and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned (defined as a union between one man and one woman); a trans visitor travelling with a partner has no recognition, and public affection can be prosecuted under the public-morals provisions.

sources.summary: ILGA World 'Our Identities Under Arrest' (2023) - global report on laws criminalising LGBT people; the fetched copy contained no extractable text at research time (image-based PDF).

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Central African Republic: no legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons; marriage constitutionally defined as a 'union between one man and one woman' with same-sex marriage banned; legal gender recognition not permitted; LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the military; criminalisation of same-sex activity in public pushed the community underground, and there were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for the Central African Republic: documents extrajudicial killings, torture, rape by security forces and Seleka rebels, harsh prison conditions - general human-rights context with limited LGBT-specific content.

Erasing 76 Crimes / ILGA overview (20 May 2019): in the Central African Republic same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, but Article 85 of the criminal code criminalises 'attacks on public morals' — public same-sex acts carry harsher penalties than other moral offences. SOGI issues remain taboo and seen as 'imported from Europe'/'contrary to African values'; CAR received two UPR recommendations (SOGI non-discrimination, improving the situation of sexual minorities).

UN OHCHR summary of stakeholders' submissions for the CAR's UPR (45th session, Jan 2024): covers international obligations, national human-rights framework, institutional infrastructure - includes SOGI-related stakeholder recommendations.
